content.text:
## Directions a matrix cannot turn

Every square matrix $A$ moves most vectors off their line. A few special vectors only get **longer or shorter**:

$$
A v = \lambda v, \qquad v \neq 0
$$

The scalar $\lambda$ is the *eigenvalue*; $v$ is an *eigenvector*. Geometrically, $v$ spans a line that $A$ maps into itself.

### Why the determinant shows up

Move everything to one side:

$$
(A - \lambda I)\,v = 0
$$

So $v$ lives in the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. A nonzero kernel is exactly what a determinant of zero detects, which turns a search over vectors into a polynomial in one unknown.

| Object | What it is | How you find it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eigenvalue $\lambda$ | a stretch factor | roots of $\det(A - \lambda I)$ |
| Eigenvector $v$ | a direction kept | $\ker(A - \lambda I)$ |
| Eigenspace $E_\lambda$ | all of them, plus $0$ | a subspace, so it has a basis |

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Av = λv] --> B["(A − λI)v = 0"]
  B --> C[v in the kernel]
  C --> D["det(A − λI) = 0"]
```

You can check a candidate numerically too:

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
values, vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(values)          # [3. 1.]
print(A @ vectors[:, 0] - values[0] * vectors[:, 0])  # ~[0, 0]
```

Your notes call the kernel $\ker$, so I will too.

arguments.question: In your own words: why does a vector $v \neq 0$ with $Av = \lambda v$ force $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$?
arguments.correctAnswer: $Av = \lambda v$ rearranges to $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$. A nonzero $v$ in the kernel means $A - \lambda I$ is not injective, so it is not invertible, and a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Hence $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
arguments.details: A short argument is enough: two or three sentences.

content.text:
Right: the kernel argument is the whole reason. One detail to keep: "not invertible" and "determinant zero" are the same statement **only for square matrices**, which $A - \lambda I$ always is.

### From the equation to numbers

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the characteristic polynomial has a shortcut:

$$
\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\,\lambda + \det A
$$

1. Read off the trace and determinant.
2. Solve the quadratic for $\lambda$.
3. For each root, solve $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ to get the eigenline.

> The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant their product. That is a fast check on any answer.

Before we compute, make a prediction.

arguments.question: Take $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Before computing anything: which two directions do you expect to stay on their own line, and roughly how much will each be stretched? Say why.
arguments.correctAnswer: The matrix is symmetric with equal diagonal entries, so the diagonal $(1,1)$ and the antidiagonal $(1,-1)$ are the natural candidates. $A(1,1) = (3,3)$, stretched by $3$; $A(1,-1) = (1,-1)$, stretched by $1$. The characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$ confirms $\lambda = 1, 3$.
arguments.details: A guess with a reason is worth more than a computed answer here.
